nameStory: The name "periwinkle" comes from the Latin "pervinca," meaning "to bind around" or "entwine," referring to how this plant's trailing stems wrap around and bind together as they spread. The "greater" part of the name simply distinguishes it from its smaller cousin, lesser periwinkle, though both share those distinctive five-petaled blue flowers that gardeners have treasured for centuries.
description: Greater periwinkle is a low-growing evergreen groundcover that spreads by trailing stems along the ground. It forms dense mats about 10 inches tall with glossy, oval leaves and cheerful blue flowers that look like tiny pinwheels. Originally from the Mediterranean, this hardy plant has escaped from gardens throughout New England, where it can spread indefinitely once established. Its tough, waxy leaves stay green year-round, making it easily recognizable even in winter.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five flat, blue petals arranged like a pinwheel, each petal appearing slightly twisted or windmill-like, blooming mainly in spring but sporadically through summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Glossy, oval leaves about 2-3 inches long that feel thick and waxy to the touch, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem and staying green all winter

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spreading mats by sending out long trailing stems that root where they touch the ground, creating thick carpets that can cover large areas

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Long, flexible green stems that trail along the ground and feel smooth but sturdy when handled, often rooting at the joints where they contact soil

habitat: Look for greater periwinkle in shaded areas near old homesites, abandoned gardens, and woodland edges where it has escaped cultivation. It thrives in partial to full shade and tolerates various soil types, often forming extensive colonies under trees or along stone walls. In New England, it's most commonly found in disturbed woodlands and residential areas where it was originally planted as groundcover.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming time with abundant blue pinwheel flowers appearing among the glossy green leaves. New growth emerges bright green and tender.
seasonality.summer: Flowers become sporadic but leaves remain lush and green. This is when the plant does most of its spreading via trailing stems.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may resume briefly in cooler weather. Leaves stay green and glossy while most other groundcover plants begin to fade.
seasonality.winter: One of the few groundcovers that stays bright green under snow. The evergreen leaves make it easily identifiable even in the depths of winter.

funFact: Greater periwinkle was so valued by ancient cultures that it was called the "flower of immortality" - not just because it stays green all winter, but because a single plant can theoretically live forever by continuously cloning itself through its rooting stems, making some colonies potentially hundreds of years old!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with lesser periwinkle, but greater periwinkle has noticeably larger leaves (2-3 inches vs. 1 inch) and flowers. Memory trick: "Greater" means bigger leaves that you can really grab and feel - they're substantial and waxy, while lesser periwinkle's leaves feel small and delicate.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its innocent garden appearance, greater periwinkle is considered invasive in some New England areas because it can smother native wildflowers with its dense, ever-expanding mats. Many gardeners are now choosing native alternatives, but established colonies often persist for decades even after homes are abandoned.
compareHints: Greater periwinkle is much larger than lesser periwinkle in every way - bigger leaves, bigger flowers, and more aggressive spreading habit. Lesser periwinkle forms neater, more controlled patches with dainty 1-inch leaves, while greater periwinkle creates bold swaths with substantial 2-3 inch leaves that feel distinctly thick and waxy. Both stay green in winter, but greater periwinkle's robust appearance makes it unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Lesser periwinkle is much more common in New England than greater periwinkle (Vinca major), which has noticeably larger leaves (over 2 inches long) and more upright growth reaching 8-12 inches tall.
